What is in the template

  • Cover page with provider, client, reference, date and validity date.
  • Executive summary with an at-a-glance box.

  • Phased approach with a Gantt-style timeline, activities and a milestone per phase.

  • Assumptions, three cumulative pricing options (one recommended), payment schedule, terms placeholders and a signature block.

How to fill it in

How the proposal is meant to read

Clients rarely read proposals end to end. They read the summary, look at the price and check whether you understood the problem. This template is built for that: the answer comes first, the evidence follows, and the options are laid out so the client can say yes to one of them. The sample example is a fictional logistics client; it is there to show the level of detail, not to be kept.

Step 1: Cover and reference

Replace the provider and client names, the contact, the date and a reference number. Set a validity date (30 days is common) so the price is not open-ended. Change the title to the outcome the client wants rather than the activity you will do: “Cut quote-to-cash to five days” says more than “Process improvement project”.

Step 2: Write the executive summary last

Two short paragraphs: the client’s problem in their own terms, then what you propose, the outcome and the price range. The three bullets in the box should be the outcome, what is different about your approach and the options and prices. Label outcomes the client has stated as the client’s targets, not guarantees; you cannot promise results you do not control.

Step 3: Show you listened

The “what we heard” table lists the client’s needs in their words, for example speed, accuracy, control and timing. Use phrases from your discovery call. State that you will test these in the first phase, so that nobody treats an unverified claim as fact. If you have not spoken to the client yet, do that before sending a proposal.

Step 4: Phases, timeline and deliverables

Aim for three to five phases, each with start and end weeks, three activities and a milestone the client signs off. Phases can overlap. Then list deliverables so each one can be checked: what it is, what form it takes and how it is accepted. A deliverable that cannot be inspected will be argued about later. Make sure total weeks, phase names and deliverable numbers agree everywhere in the document.

Step 5: Price three options

Offer a smaller, a recommended and a fuller option, with each one including everything in the previous one so nothing is hidden. Prices should rise. Mark the one you recommend and give a reason. The sample prices and currency are placeholders: replace them with your own fees and add whether they include VAT or sales tax. State the payment schedule, such as 30% on signature, 40% at a milestone and 30% on acceptance.

Step 6: Assumptions, terms and signature

Write five to eight assumptions that can be tested: access to people and systems, who approves work and how fast, what is excluded and how travel is charged. The terms table contains bracketed placeholders for payment, change control, intellectual property, confidentiality, liability and governing law. These are legal matters: ask a solicitor or attorney to complete them or attach your standard terms. Leave the client signature blank.

Finish

Search the document for the square brackets and replace or remove all of them. Save as PDF to send; keep the Word file to edit. See the proposal and SOW guide for more on structure and pricing.

Frequently asked questions

Is this consulting proposal template free?

Yes. Download the Word and PDF files without signing up.

Is it legal advice or a contract?

No. It is a commercial proposal. The terms section holds placeholders that a lawyer should complete.

Can I change the currency?

Yes. The sample text uses placeholder amounts. Replace each price and the currency name in the pricing table and the summary.

Is it A4 or US Letter?

A4. If you are in the US, change Layout > Size to Letter in Word and check the tables.

What is the difference between a proposal and a statement of work?

A proposal sells the work and lets the client choose. A statement of work is the agreed scope. See the statement of work template.
